root_cause.sentence: The storm cut 150 lines, but the first overload is the heat's: the Jacksonville 64 transformer is already at 239% of its rating before the storm and 256% after.

hospitals.assumption: A hospital counts as on backup power when the substation nearest it in the synthetic model lost at least 60% of its load. Real hospitals have their own feeders, generators and priority restoration.

cost.who_pays: 2 cents to 17 cents per household per month (illustrative)

assumptions.note: How long the lost load stays dark (estimated from the incident's size, a rule of thumb).
10,982 MW of customers dark for about 50.4 hours (estimated from the incident's size) at LBNL's value of lost load by customer class, weighted by U.S. sales (2024 dollars).
The upgrades that stop the cascade, priced by voltage class and length: reconductoring to a new line (Black & Veatch, 2014 dollars raised to 2024); transformers at $7,250 to $13,450 per MVA.
Illustrative: the upgrades paid back over 40 years at 7% a year, spread over the state's households; low, households pay their share of sales; high, all of it. Who really pays is up to regulators.

fixes.label: Change the hour
fixes.tradeoff: The grid fits at 3 AM and 9 AM but not at 130% of the summer peak load; the heat itself can't be scheduled away.

fixes.label: Upgrade the lines
fixes.tradeoff: New equipment on 30 lines and 10 transformers (170.3 km of line). It stops the cascade, but the 4.34 million people (estimate) the storm cut off stay dark until the downed lines are rebuilt.

no_fix.sentence: No fix exists for about 4.34 million people (estimate). Even with unlimited line capacity and no data center, the damage cuts them off from the power plants that could serve them; only rebuilding the downed lines brings them back. Every fix family was checked, and the best saves at most 24% of the outage.

recovery.method_note: line limits applied: a controlled-pickup LP (generators re-dispatched, every line within its rating; loop flows not modeled)
